transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-08
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Lara Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Redwood CSM), Daniel Park (Head of ML, Spectral), Erin Walsh (PM), Samir Patel (SRE), Rita Gomez (Data Scientist)

Summary:
Quick weekly POC check-in focused on recent regression signal after moving to quantized model variant, guardrail false-positive uptick, and planning a probing experiment and canary run. Agreed to run a 2k-sample regression test and share scoring breakdown. Next steps and owners captured.

Topics:
- Regression spike after 8-bit quantization
- Scoring rubric drift and false positive examples
- Guardrail tuning (safety + hallucination thresholds)
- Canary and staging plan for Dedicated pool
- Security/compliance questions (SOC 2, KMS)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Lara Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, um, we wanted to start with the regression signal you saw last week after you switched to the 8-bit profile. Marco and I have sample logs and an initial hypothesis.
[00:18] Daniel Park: Yeah, hey Lara. Thanks. We did, we saw a bump in false positives in the customer intent classifier — like the model started flagging normal webchat as "policy" on a few prompts. We rolled back but we'd like to understand root cause.
[00:33] Marco Diaz: Right, so quick caveat — transcript caveat — our perf numbers are from the Dedicatedy test pool, sorry, Dedicated pool, and we used the new quant kernel. There's a couple of places quantization can change tokenization alignment and scoring thresholds.
[00:48] Rita Gomez: And to add, some of the flagged prompts are short, like 3-4 tokens, and the kv‑cache prefetch behavior seems different when the sequence is short, so maybe the context window handling is slightly off.
[01:05] Samir Patel: Just to clarify, are you saying this was only on Dedicated or also on hosted API? We run a mix — staging uses your hosted endpoint.
[01:14] Marco Diaz: Good question. The regression was reproduced on the Dedicated quantized variant only; hosted with the same base model but non-quant (float16) didn't show the spike. But, caveat, hosted routing used a slightly different tokenizer config — so small differences there.
[01:32] Erin Walsh: So what's our immediate risk? If we move forward with canary, what guardrails do we need to put in place? We don't want production chatter to get flagged.
[01:42] Priya Singh: From an ops pov we'll want a gradual ramp with fallback to float16 model if flags exceed threshold, and a runbook for rollback.
[01:50] Lara Chen: Exactly. Marco, can you walk through the hypothesis?
[01:55] Marco Diaz: Sure — hypothesis one: quantization introduced slight logit shifts on rare token sequences which, with the current scoring rubric, push borderline cases over the safety threshold. Hypothesis two: prefix caching for short sequences is behaving differently because the KV cache alignments change with our internal token merge, causing context truncation. Hypothesis three: prompt canonicalization differences — e.g., whitespace/linebreak handling — were amplified after quant compression.
[02:25] Daniel Park: Hmm. Could this also be an artifact of our prompt engineering? We recently trimmed the prompt to save tokens, that may make the examples more ambiguous.
[02:33] Rita Gomez: We did trim. I think we removed a disambiguation sentence. I'll own that as an action — send the pre/post prompt versions.
[02:40] Lara Chen: Great. For diagnostics, Marco proposed a probing experiment: run a 2,000-sample regression where we compare float16 vs 8-bit quant on the same prompts, collect per-token confidence, delta logits, and the scoring rubric outputs. Marco, timeline?
[02:55] Marco Diaz: I can spin that up in our Dedicated test pool, it should take about 48 hours to run and we'll dump a CSV with token-level diffs. I'll include examples where the safety signal flips.
[03:08] Samir Patel: We need to ensure logs don't include PII in test samples, we'll scrub before you ingest.
[03:14] Lara Chen: Agreed — anonymize via hashing.
[03:18] Erin Walsh: On evaluation, I'd like us to add a separate 'edge-case' column in the rubric so we can track when short prompts cause flips.
[03:26] Rita Gomez: Noted.
[03:28] Marco Diaz: One nuance — the scoring rubric currently uses a threshold at 0.7 for policy flags; a 0.03 shift in logits can push some 0.68s to 0.71. We can either adjust threshold or sharpen the guardrail with additional contextual checks.
[03:44] Daniel Park: Adjusting threshold is scary though, because we might reduce sensitivity on real bad cases.
[03:49] Lara Chen: Right, so our recommended approach is to do the probing experiment first, produce an ROC-style curve, then decide whether to change thresholds or add secondary checks (like rule-based heuristics).
[03:58] Priya Singh: From a release perspective, we can set an auto-fallback policy in the routing layer: if model-level safety flips > 0.5% of queries in a 1-hour window, route to float16. That preserves uptime.
[04:12] Samir Patel: And what about cost? Dedicated quant runs save us like 25% per token, so we don't want to lose that unless absolutely necessary.
[04:21] Lara Chen: Understood — that's where intelligent routing comes in. We can set a cost/safety policy. Also Marco will include token-cost deltas in the 2k run.
[04:29] Erin Walsh: Can we also capture latency differences? We observed slightly lower p95 on quant but don't have a controlled test.
[04:36] Marco Diaz: Yes, latency, p50/p95/p99, and tail behavior will be in the report — note though, quantization sometimes trades off jitter for lower mean. We'll show the distribution.
[04:46] Daniel Park: On compliance, we need to see SOC 2 docs and the KMS/HSM flow if we go Dedicated or Private. Our security team requires SSO (SAML) and audit logs retention for 1 year.
[05:00] Lara Chen: We'll share SOC 2 and our KMS integration guide; Redwood supports customer-managed keys in Private and Dedicated via KMS/HSM integrations. We'll attach the compliance pack after the call.
[05:12] Priya Singh: I'll add that to the next steps — send the compliance pack.
[05:16] Rita Gomez: Back to the probe — how granular are the diffs? Token-level? Could you include the tokenization mismatch cases?
[05:24] Marco Diaz: Yes token-level, and a note when token counts differ due to tokenizer variation. Expect an "alignment" column that'll show the origin tokenization and any merges.
[05:33] [00:05:40] Speaker overlap / cross talk: Daniel: oh — also, small note, some of our test harness uses tf-serving wrappers, not your SDK; will that affect results?
[05:42] Marco Diaz: Good flag — Ideally we'll run the Dedicated regression via Redwood SDK to remove wrapper differences. But we can also reproduce via your harness if you'd like parity.
[05:52] Erin Walsh: For scheduling, what windows do you need?
[05:55] Marco Diaz: Any time this week or next; the 2k job itself is short but we want a clean environment — propose Thursday evening PT for the run, results Friday morning.
[06:05] Daniel Park: Thursday works. We'll scrub data and send sample set by Friday EOD?
[06:12] Rita Gomez: We can send 200 labeled edge-case prompts by Friday (that's the ones we think flipped).
[06:18] Lara Chen: Perfect.
[06:20] [00:06:20] Lara: Okay moving on, prompt set and scoring — Rita, can you summarize the scoring rubric changes you made last week?
[06:28] Rita Gomez: Sure — we tightened the heuristics to reduce false negatives, specifically we lowered the threshold for semantic similarity matching and added a syntactic pattern for phone numbers. That probably increased sensitivity and interacts with the model scoring.
[06:40] Daniel Park: Right, so combined with quant shift it's compounding.
[06:44] Marco Diaz: A common mitigation is to normalise heuristic outputs or run a small ensemble: if model flag + heuristic flag => hard block; if model flag only and below new higher threshold => score with secondary classifier.
[06:59] Erin Walsh: That ensemble approach seems reasonable. What's the lift to implement?
[07:03] Marco Diaz: We can prototype a secondary classifier in a couple of days using your labeled set — likely a logistic regressor over the model score + heuristic signals. It won't take much infra.
[07:13] Priya Singh: Meanwhile, I'll prepare a rollback playbook and routing policy in the console and share the draft.
[07:20] Lara Chen: Great. Also we should capture a set of 'ground truth' passes so we can compute precision/recall differences — Rita, can you mark those?
[07:26] Rita Gomez: Yep, I'll produce a golden set of ~500 items.
[07:30] [00:07:30] Marco: Quick question about the canary: do you prefer canary traffic to be synthetic test traffic or a shadow of real traffic?
[07:39] Daniel Park: We'd like a small percentage (0.5%) of real traffic shadowed, plus synthetic targeted tests, so we can see real-world signals without impacting users.
[07:48] Samir Patel: For shadowing we'll need logs to be redacted. Also ensure we don't send PII to Redwood logs — either we hash or we send minimal features.
[07:58] Lara Chen: Agreed, we'll accept hashed payloads.
[08:02] Erin Walsh: On the metrics dashboard, can we get per-route breakdowns and alert thresholds?
[08:07] Priya Singh: Yes, the Console supports per-route SLOs and alerting hooks. I'll drop a dashboard template.
[08:13] Daniel Park: Can we get token-level cost reporting? Important to show the delta if we revert to float16.
[08:19] Marco Diaz: We'll include cost per request with token counts and estimated monthly extrapolation.
[08:24] Lara Chen: Now quick callout — we heard about intermittent KL divergence in long contexts in some of your earlier tests; is that still an issue?
[08:33] Rita Gomez: Not in float16, but with quant, long contexts like 1,200 tokens show slightly higher perplexity.
[08:40] Marco Diaz: That ties to kernel selection and compilation choices — sometimes the quant kernel approximates attention differently for very long sequences. We'll include a kernel-level note.
[08:50] Daniel Park: Okay makes sense.
[08:52] [00:08:52] Lara: Alright, let's capture decisions: run 2k probe; keep routing fallback; produce ROC & token diffs; don't change threshold until we see probe results; prepare canary (0.5% shadow + synthetic).
[09:05] Erin Walsh: One more question: if the probe shows only a handful of pathological prompts causing flips, can we do prompt-level patching?
[09:14] Marco Diaz: Yes — we support prompt-level overrides and prefix caching to force a safer canonicalization. But that can get messy at scale.
[09:22] Daniel Park: We'll prioritize a small set of overrides if needed.
[09:25] Priya Singh: I'll create the canary runbook with those conditional steps.
[09:30] Lara Chen: Any blockers on your side?
[09:33] Daniel Park: Security still needs the SOC 2 pack, and they want a sample audit log format.
[09:39] Lara Chen: We'll send both. Marco will attach the sample redacted log.
[09:44] Rita Gomez: Also request: can you include tokenizer version in the report? We saw differences between spm v1 and v2.
[09:51] Marco Diaz: Yes, tokenizer version and token alignment will be in the CSV.
[09:56] Erin Walsh: For ownership — who owns the scoring rubric change if we decide to revert?
[10:01] Daniel Park: Spectral owns the business logic changes; Redwood will provide the instrumentation and operational recommendations.
[10:09] Lara Chen: Noted. Alright, let's run through concrete due dates — Rita will send edge cases + pre/post prompts by 2026-04-10; Lara to send compliance docs by 2026-04-09; Marco to run the probe starting 2026-04-15 and share results 2026-04-17; Priya to schedule canary for week of 2026-04-20.
[10:28] Erin Walsh: Sounds good.
[10:30] [00:10:30] Closing:
Lara Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up in the thread with links to the test harness, the prompt CSV template, and the runbook.
Daniel Park: Thanks, appreciate it.

End of transcript.
